title: Case Study: CommonSpirit Health grows healthcare talent from within with LAUNCH
summary: How CommonSpirit Health uses its LAUNCH earn-and-learn apprenticeship, powered by Stepful, to build and keep allied health staff from its own communities.
body_markdown:
CommonSpirit Health, one of the largest health systems in the country with 160,000 employees and more than 2,600 care sites across 24 states, has partnered with Stepful to scale its LAUNCH (Leveraging Apprenticeships & Upskilling for New Careers in Healthcare) Program, an earn-and-learn apprenticeship for allied health roles. Through LAUNCH, learners from the local community and existing employees are paid and trained on the job, at the clinics where they'll go on to work.


## **The challenge**


Healthcare is facing a projected shortage of more than 100,000 workers by 2028, with allied health roles among the hardest hit. CommonSpirit felt that pressure firsthand: in Kentucky, its physician group grew 254% in a single year, and medical assistant hiring did not keep up.


CommonSpirit set out to build a steady supply of allied health staff from the communities it already serves, and to keep the people it trains. The early results are encouraging. Medical assistants hired through the apprenticeship stay with CommonSpirit about 19% longer on average than other MAs.


## **The solution**


Through LAUNCH, CommonSpirit covers 100% of tuition and pays apprentices an hourly wage while they train. Stepful runs live, teacher-led online classes, so every class trains to the same standard at every site.


> “Stepful stood out for its live, instructor-led online courses and a platform that supports preceptors, administrators, and students. As we scale LAUNCH, we need the same standard across sites. Stepful builds that consistency into our program.”


**Ricci Barton** , Workforce Development, CommonSpirit Health


## **How LAUNCH works**


Clinic leaders apply for an apprentice and help pick the candidate. Each apprenticeship is then posted as a full-time role, open to both current staff and outside candidates. After practicing at home with training kits, apprentices train at the clinic where they'll work, which doubles as a built-in interview.


Throughout the program, Stepful and CommonSpirit's education team check in every two weeks, run mock scenarios and work with on-site coaches. Clinic leaders, preceptors and apprentices are all surveyed mid-program and at the end to confirm their hiring needs are met. Programs live today include Medical Assistant, Surgical Tech, Patient Care Tech and Phlebotomy.


> “It's almost like a 6-month interview. You really get to learn that person throughout that time frame. That's the benefit of building talent internally: they're learning in our own clinical walls, with our teams and our patients, so by the time they're hired, they already know how we work.”


**[Magaly Torres](https://www.linkedin.com/in/magaly-torres-128b1a226/)** , Regional MA Clinical Educator, CommonSpirit Health


## **Backed by Stepful results**


The partnership is backed by Stepful's results nationwide: a 90% completion rate for Stepful-sponsored learners, a 94% CCMA pass rate compared with 82% nationally, and more than 42,000 graduates to date. Every partnership also comes with a completion guarantee, so 100% of an employer's investment results in completion. If a learner drops out, the employer gets a seat in the next cohort at no extra cost.


## **What's next**


CommonSpirit plans to grow LAUNCH from Colorado to all 24 states, working alongside its Talent Acquisition team to target the hardest-to-fill roles. It is also partnering with peers in the Healthcare Anchor Network on how to create better pathways into sustainable healthcare careers.


Stepful offers employer-sponsored programs for Medical Assistant, Pharmacy Tech, Surgical Tech, Sterile Processing, Patient Care Tech and Plus, Phlebotomy and Practical Nursing. Learn how Stepful helps health systems build their own talent pipeline at[stepful.com/for-employers](https://www.stepful.com/for-employers) .
